papers.title_in_file: First-Orderized ResearchCyc : Expressivity and Efﬁciency in a Common-Sense Ontology
papers.what_it_is: A 2005 AAAI-workshop paper that translates about 90% of the ResearchCyc knowledge base into first-order logic and times three first-order theorem provers against Cyc's own inference engine on 8 queries.

assertions.value: The authors report that ResearchCyc consists of 1,074,484 assertions in a language of 122,658 symbols (not including strings or numbers), against 60,000 axioms over 20,000 terms for the IEEE Suggested Upper Merged Ontology.
quotes: consists of 1,074,484 assertions in a language of 122,658 symbols (not including strings or numbers)
the IEEE Suggested Upper Merged Ontology (Niles & Pease 2001) consists of 60,000 axioms over 20,000 terms
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the size of the knowledge base they translated, in Section 1.

assertions.value: The authors report that the first-orderized (FOLified) ResearchCyc KB consisted of 1,253,117 axioms over 132,116 symbols (not including strings or numbers), and that translating axiom schemata exactly increases the size of the representation.
quotes: Our ﬁnal FOLiﬁed ResearchCyc KB consisted of 1,253,117 axioms over 132,116 symbols (not including strings or numbers).
but with an increase in the size of the representation (both the number of symbols and axioms)
assertions.certainty_reason: A measured size from one translation run by the authors.
assertions.reader_inference: Against 1,074,484 source assertions, the translated KB holds about 17% more axioms; the paper does not state this ratio.

assertions.value: The authors report that their FOLifier translated 960,327 of the 1,074,484 ResearchCyc assertions successfully, and that Table 1 lists, for the rest, the reason no translation was possible and the number of assertions affected.
quotes: Overall 960,327 (out of 1,074,484) assertions were translated successfully.
we list the reasons why a translation was not possible and the number of assertions for which that reason applies
assertions.certainty_reason: A measured count from the authors' own tool on one KB snapshot.
assertions.reader_inference: 960,327 of 1,074,484 is about 89.4%, which matches the abstract's 'around 90%'; the paper does not state the figure.

assertions.value: The authors report in the translation statistics table that the largest untranslatable categories were UNBOUNDED ARITY FUNCTION (77756 assertions), META-SENTENCE (54209) and META-VARIABLE (18923); the last reason listed is VARIABLE ARITY PREDICATE, at 0. The text layer prints the reason names and the counts as two separate lists, so the pairing of name to count follows list order.
assertions.anchor: Table 1, p.4 (text layer holds names and counts in separate lists)
quotes: FOL untranslatability reason UNBOUNDED ARITY FUNCTION META-SENTENCE META-VARIABLE
assertions.certainty_reason: A measured table from one run; the pairing of names to counts is read from list order in the text layer.
assertions.reader_inference: The listed counts sum to about 186,000, more than the 114,157 assertions left untranslated (1,074,484 minus 960,327); the paper does not explain the difference, so an assertion may carry more than one reason.

assertions.value: The authors state that they use the term 'higher-order' to mean any feature beyond ordinary first-order logic, such as a context system or quantification over predicates, and that the term signifies any conceivable extension to the usual syntactic restrictions of FOL.
quotes: we will use the term ”higher-order” to mean any feature beyond ordinary ﬁrst-order logic, like a context system or quantiﬁcation over predicates
it signiﬁes any conceivable extension to the usual syntactic restrictions of FOL: variable-arity predicates, sentences as arguments, etc.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors define their own use of the term in Section 1 and again in Section 3.

assertions.value: The authors state in the abstract that their results indicate the use of higher-order logic is not essential to the representability of common-sense knowledge, but greatly improves the efficiency of reasoning.
quotes: Our results indicate that, while the use of higher-order logic is not essential to the representability of common-sense knowledge, it greatly improves the efﬁciency of reasoning.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim; Section 5 calls the experiments preliminary and Section 6 says the representability test is not yet done.
assertions.reader_inference: The abstract is stronger than the body: Section 6 says the untranslated 10% 'may form the core of Cyc's ontology' and that representability still needs a query-based test.

assertions.value: The authors state that, counted by axioms, they translated around 90% of the axioms, but that the other 10% that remained untranslated may form the core of Cyc's ontology; they say a large corpus of queries from the ResearchCyc test suite is needed to verify this.
quotes: sheer number, we were able to translate around 90% of the axioms. However, the other 10% of axioms that remained untranslated may form the core of Cyc’s ontology.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state this limit on their own translation result in Section 6.

assertions.value: The authors state that the percentage of queries that both ResearchCyc and any ATP system can answer would measure how much of the information content of the KB is translated and how much inferential power carries over to FOL; they do not report this percentage.
quotes: The percentage of queries that can be answered by both ResearchCyc and any ATP system gives a measure of how much of the information content of the KB is actually translated
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors name a measurement they did not make, in Section 6.

assertions.value: The authors cite Boolos (1984) for two sentences that cannot be represented in a logic without predicate quantification: 'Some critics admire only one another.' and 'Some of Fianchetto's men went into the warehouse unaccompanied by anyone else.' They note the second is non-firstorderizable if 'anyone else' means anyone not in the group of Fianchetto's men who went into the warehouse.
quotes: Boolos (Boolos 1984) discusses two sentences that cannot be represented in a logic without predicate quantiﬁcation (non-ﬁrstorderizable)
1. Some critics admire only one another.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to Boolos (1984), not shown in this paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that it is widely believed that a complete specification of what is understood to be common-sense knowledge requires some kind of higher-order features, and that a second reason for higher-order constructs is succinct representation that specialized reasoning methods can use.
quotes: it is widely believed that a complete speciﬁcation of what is understood to be “common-sense knowledge” requires some kind of higher-order features
the ability to represent knowledge succinctly and in a form that can be taken advantage of by specialized reasoning methods
assertions.certainty_reason: A belief the authors report without evidence.

assertions.value: The authors describe ResearchCyc's context system as follows: each assertion is associated with a microtheory (mt) that determines its context; microtheories form a hierarchy in which each has access to all the assertions in its parents; the language is extended with the modal operator ist(k, phi) to say phi is true in context k; and the predicate genlMt declares one microtheory a child of another.
quotes: Each assertion in the KB is associated with a microtheory (“mt”) that determines its context.
with each microtheory having access to all the assertions in its parents.
extending the language with the modal operator ist(k, ϕ)(“is true”) to express that the assertion ϕ is true in the context k
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors define the context system they translate, in Section 3.1.

assertions.value: The authors describe two methods for handling microtheories in pure first-order logic: treat each context as a separate module and compile the required ones into a single flat KB (the approach of SUMO), or approximate the ist modality with an mtVisible predicate so that each assertion is conditioned on mtVisible of its microtheory.
quotes: There are two methods for handling microtheories in pure ﬁrst-order logic.
One is to treat each context as a separate module, choose at inference time which modules are required, and compile them into a single ﬂat KB.
A more sophisticated scheme is to approximate the ist modality with an mtVisible predicate.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors define the two translation schemes in Section 3.1.

assertions.value: The authors state that both context-handling methods cannot represent inter-contextual reasoning: the module method has no means of referring to other contexts, and in the mtVisible method the translation of 'context k1 knows axiom phi is true in context k2' as mtVisible(k1) implies (mtVisible(k2) implies phi) is equivalent to mtVisible(k2) implies (mtVisible(k1) implies phi), which was not intended.
quotes: Both techniques mentioned above have one limitation: the inability to represent inter-contextual reasoning.
In the module-based method there are no means of referring to other contexts.
which was not intended at all.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state this limit of their translation in Section 3.1.
assertions.reader_inference: The equivalence of the two implication orders is a propositional identity, so the stated argument holds.

assertions.value: The authors report that their tool uses a combination of both context methods: in general each assertion is prefixed with the mtVisible condition for its microtheory, but assertions from UniversalVocabularyMt or BaseKB are translated without adding the mtVisible predicate, since they are visible to practically every query.
quotes: Our translation tool uses a combination of both methods.
when the assertion is from either UniversalVocabularyMt or BaseKB, then it is FOLiﬁed without adding the mtVisible predicate at all
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state how their tool treats contexts, in Section 3.1.

assertions.value: The authors state that some assertions (for example axiom schemata) could be translated precisely without loss of semantics, while others (for example contexts) could only be translated approximately.
quotes: In some cases (e.g. axiom schemata), the assertions could be translated precisely without any loss of semantics
In other cases (e.g. contexts) only an approximate translation could be made.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the limit of their translation in Section 1.

assertions.value: The authors report that the FOLifier creates a unique unary predicate for each Cyc collection, translating genls (Fruit PlantPart) as for all x, Fruit(x) implies PlantPart(x); reified collection-denoting terms such as (JuvenileFn Human) are handled by ignoring the functional nature of the term and concatenating the function and argument names into a new predicate.
quotes: The FOLiﬁer creates a unique unary predicate for each collection, e.g. Fruit(x), PlantPart(x).
we ignore the functional nature of the term and simply create a new predicate by concatenating the names of the function and its argument(s)
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state how their tool translates the genls hierarchy, in Section 3.2.

assertions.value: The authors state that using unary predicates for collections has the potential to make resolution-style inference easier because there is less choice of literals to resolve on, and that it is assumed theorem-prover heuristics are optimized for type hierarchies expressed as unary predicates. No measurement of this effect is reported.
quotes: This has the potential to make resolution-style inference easier because there is less choice of literals to resolve on
it is assumed that the heuristics of theorem provers are generally optimized for type hierarchies being expressed as unary predicates
assertions.certainty_reason: An author assumption without evidence in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that pseudo-higher-order constructs such as TransitivePred and relationAllExists are called rule macro predicates in ResearchCyc, and that it is usually straightforward to convert them into FOL by replacing the literal with a first-order axiom schema; argIsa assertions can likewise be translated, for example as for all x, y, performedBy(x, y) implies Action(x).
quotes: pseudo-higher-order constructs such as the above are called rule macro predicates
it is usually straightforward to convert these into FOL by replacing the literal with a ﬁrst-order axiom schema
∀x∀y[performedBy(x, y) ⇒Action(x)]
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state how their tool translates these constructs, in Section 3.3.

assertions.value: The authors state that when the arity of a predicate or function is bounded by a small number (for example Meter, which takes 1 or 2 arguments), it can be translated into FOL by suffixing the name with the arity; where the arity is fundamentally unbounded (for example TheSet), no straightforward translation seems to exist, with the different predicate on n arguments as an exception, translated into O(n squared) inequality relations. The text layer prints the example of the suffixed name as missing after 'i.e.'.
quotes: the Cyc function Meter can take either 1 or 2 arguments
In many cases, for example TheSet, the arity is fundamentally unbounded. In these cases, no straightforward translation seems to exist.
can be translated into O(n2) inequality relations
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state a limit of their translation in Section 3.4.

assertions.value: The authors state that Cyc's exceptFor and exceptWhen predicates are used to give Cyc non-monotonic behavior, that translating them could add the exception conditions as negated literals in the antecedent of the excepted rule but the general case is more difficult (and there can be problems when the assertion and exception are in different microtheories), and that their FOLifier currently does not handle exceptions.
quotes: Exception assertions like the above are used to give Cyc non-monotonic behavior.
as negated literals in the antecedent of the excepted rule. In the general case this is more difﬁcult to handle.
Currently, our FOLiﬁer does not handle exceptions.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state a limit of their tool in Section 3.5.

assertions.value: The authors state that some untranslated assertions were due to Lambda and Kappa, since function-denoting functions and predicate-denoting functions are inherently non-firstorderizable; that variable arity predicates with an upper bound are in principle translatable but the initial FOLifier handled only fixed-arity relations; and that FUNCTION ARG CONSTRAINT assertions are not currently handled.
quotes: since function-denoting functions and predicate-denoting functions are inherently non-ﬁrstorderizable
our initial FOLiﬁer implementation only handled ﬁxed-arity relations
Our FOLiﬁer implementation does not currently handle these.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state limits of their tool in Section 3.6.

assertions.value: The authors describe the Cyc Inference Engine as a higher-order theorem prover optimized for the Cyc KB that is incomplete, non-monotonic, handles context reasoning natively, is highly modular (including meta-reasoning and meta-metareasoning modules), handles theory revisions with only limited local recompilation, and has truth maintenance always on.
quotes: The Cyc Inference Engine is a higher-order theorem prover optimized for the Cyc Knowledge Base.
It is incomplete, non-monotonic, and handles context reasoning natively.
truth maintenance is always on
assertions.certainty_reason: Cycorp authors describe their own product.

assertions.value: The authors state that common-sense knowledge is more often used in relatively shallow 'needle in a haystack' proofs than in deep mathematics-style proofs, and more often for constructive proofs than proofs by contradiction; they say this influenced the design of Cyc's inference engine. No data supports the statement.
quotes: Common-sense knowledge is more often used in relatively shallow, “needle in a haystack” types of proofs than in deep mathematicsstyle proofs.
Common-sense knowledge is more often used for constructive proofs than proofs by contradiction.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim without evidence in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that Cyc's inference engine is heuristically guided and resource-bounded and trades completeness for efficiency, because common-sense knowledge is tightly interconnected and, with a very large KB, gives intractably large branching factors.
quotes: Cyc’s inference engine is heuristically guided and resource-bounded; it trades completeness for efﬁciency.
make for intractably large branching factors in inference
assertions.certainty_reason: Cycorp authors describe the design of their own product.

assertions.value: The authors state that Cyc uses a 'pandemonium' model in which hundreds to thousands of HeuristicLevel (HL) modules, each implementing an inference rule, check whether they apply to a subproblem and bid to solve it; HL modules can be added or removed without retuning or recompilation. They contrast most theorem provers as having a small handful of inference rules, usually including hyperresolution and paramodulation.
quotes: Cyc employs a “pandemonium” model in which hundreds to thousands of “HeuristicLevel (HL) modules”
HL modules can be dynamically added or removed from the system without requiring any sort of retuning or recompilation.
assertions.certainty_reason: Cycorp authors describe the architecture of their own product.

assertions.value: The authors state that for N transitive predicates Cyc can represent the knowledge in N + 1 clauses (one per predicate plus one general higher-order rule), whereas a straightforward FOL representation would need 3N clauses (a three-clause rule for each predicate); they also state that an HL module for transitive predicates does a graph walk over the KB's indexing structures that is considerably more efficient than unrestricted resolution.
quotes: Cyc can represent this knowledge in N + 1 clauses: 1 clause per predicate plus 1 very general higher-order rule.
In a straightforward FOL representation, 3N clauses would be required: 1 three-clause rule to express the transitivity of each predicate.
which is considerably more efﬁcient than performing unrestricted resolution
assertions.certainty_reason: The clause counts are the authors' own counting argument; the efficiency statement is a claim with no measurement for this module.
assertions.reader_inference: The 3N count assumes the transitivity rule is stated once per predicate rather than as one rule over a relation variable, which is what the authors call the straightforward FOL form.

assertions.value: The authors state that reasoning within a hierarchy of contexts is built into the innermost loop of Cyc's inference engine; each axiom considered for a proof is first checked for relevance to the contextual scope by graph walking of the context hierarchy (a directed graph, not necessarily acyclic), with the computation cached for common cases.
quotes: Reasoning within a hierarchy of contexts is built into the innermost loop of Cyc’s inference engine.
a directed graph, not necessarily acyclic
assertions.certainty_reason: Cycorp authors describe their own product.

assertions.value: The authors report that, with the exception of E, none of the theorem provers they tried could load more than 20% of the ResearchCyc KB without failing due to memory errors, mostly because of internal data structure limitations in the provers; E was the only program that could load the entire KB.
quotes: With the exception of E, none of the theorem provers we tried were able to load more than 20% of the ResearchCyc KB without failing due to memory errors.
E was the only program that could load the entire ResearchCyc KB
assertions.certainty_reason: A reported outcome from one set of runs on 2005-era hardware.

assertions.value: The authors report the setup: 8 common-sense queries chosen from an existing ResearchCyc test corpus before any experiment, none inherently dependent on higher-order reasoning; a randomly generated subset of the FOLified KB with less than 10% of the axioms (about 100,000 of 1,250,000), manually checked to hold every axiom needed to prove all the queries; VAMPIRE, SPASS and E run on the KB plus the negated query on an Athlon 2800 with 512 MB of RAM; SPASS was run on the OpenCyc KB instead because of licensing issues.
quotes: We selected a set of 8 common-sense queries from an existing test corpus of queries for the ResearchCyc KB.
containing less than 10% of the total number of axioms (about 100,000 out of 1,250,000)
The experiments were performed on an Athlon 2800 with 512 MB of RAM.
this was done on the OpenCyc KB, with virtually identical results
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state their experimental setup in Section 5.

assertions.value: The authors state that they did not experiment extensively with the parameter settings and heuristics the provers offered and used a uniform Set-of-Support resolution setting for all of them, and that E does not directly do Set-of-Support resolution but uses a clause weighting strategy that simulates it.
quotes: we used a uniform SetOf-Support resolution setting for all of them
E does not directly do Set-Of-Support resolution, but instead uses a clause weighting strategy that simulates it
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state a limit of their experimental setting in Section 5.1.

assertions.value: The authors report that the provers ran on a KB scaled down to under 10% while Cyc ran on the unmodified KB (over 10 times larger), and that for all queries except the last the query context was flattened into BaseKB for the provers, which saves one unit propagation step on the mtVisible literal; the last query was asked in TerrestrialFrameOfReferenceMt. They state that every deviation erred on the side of the theorem provers, speeding up their running times.
quotes: whereas Cyc’s inference engine was run on an unmodiﬁed KB (over 10 times the size of that used by the theorem provers)
we ensured that we erred on the side of the theorem provers, i.e. the changes sped up their running times
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the deviations in their testing conditions in Section 5.1.

assertions.value: The authors report in the inference experiments table the time, in seconds, for VAMPIRE, SPASS, E and Cyc on each query. For the disjointWith (HumanInfant Doctor-Medical) query they report 847.6 (VAMPIRE), 1239.1 (SPASS), 2934 (E) and 0.04 (Cyc). The text layer scrambles the rest of the table, so only the rows it holds in a clear order are stated here.
assertions.anchor: Table 2, p.6 (text layer scrambles the rows)
quotes: (disjointWith HumanInfant Doctor-Medical)
(sec.) (sec.) (sec.)
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical timing from one study, with a scrambled table layer.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer does not keep the table's row order, so the other rows cannot be assigned to queries with certainty from this layer.

assertions.value: The authors report that Cyc's performance was orders of magnitude better than the theorem provers on almost all of the queries, and that the ATP systems performed orders of magnitude more slowly than the ResearchCyc inference engine; they say they believe this validates their hypothesis that a specialized inference engine working natively with compact higher-order representations and special-purpose modules will perform better on common-sense queries than general first-order strategies, while stating that much work remains before the claim can be asserted with confidence.
quotes: The immediate observation is that Cyc’s performance is orders of magnitude better on almost all the queries.
However, much work remains to be done before this claim can be asserted with conﬁdence.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one preliminary study on 8 queries; the authors call it open to interpretation.
assertions.reader_inference: The comparison is of different systems on different KB sizes, with different settings; it does not isolate the effect of higher-order representation from the effect of Cyc's custom engine.

assertions.value: The authors report that the only query on which Cyc was within an order of magnitude of any prover was the second, the hasMembers query, because Cyc hypothesizes terms for ?X, ?Y and ?Z and runs forward inference first; 2.3 of its 2.5 seconds went to forward inference, which was unnecessary for this query, and they estimate that lazy forward inference could answer it in 0.2 seconds.
quotes: 2.3 of the 2.5 seconds are spent in forward inference, which proves to be unnecessary for this particular query
Cyc could answer the question in 0.2 seconds rather than 2.5 seconds
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study; the 0.2 second figure is the authors' estimate, not a run.

assertions.value: The authors describe how Cyc solves the disjointWith (Baseball-Ball Cube) query: an HL module marks each genls ancestor of Cube as a goal, walks up the genls graph of Baseball-Ball, and for each more general collection follows its asserted disjointWith links to check whether it reaches a goal node, with a genlMt graph walk on each link traversal. The first-order approach instead translates genls and disjointWith assertions into rules and runs a resolution-style proof search on the negated query to reach a contradiction.
quotes: First it walks up the genls graph for Cube, marking each node as a goal.
on each traversal of each link in the genls and disjointWith graphs, Cyc does another graph walk of the genlMt graph
running a resolution-style proof search will then yield a contradiction and hence a positive answer
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors describe the two procedures they compare, in Section 5.

assertions.value: The authors list alternative explanations for the timing gap that they did not rule out: the provers were not run under ideal settings and an improved clause or literal weighting strategy might make them competitive with Cyc; or the incomplete FOLification may omit axioms key to efficient proofs. They state that they hypothesize the second is not the case and plan to test it.
quotes: our tests with most theorem provers were not performed under ideal settings
It could be that with, for example, an improved clause/literal weighting strategy, these theorem provers would become competitive with Cyc.
We hypothesize that this is not the case
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state limits of their comparison in Section 5.1.

assertions.value: The authors state that at the time of publication they could not obtain the extensive results needed to draw confident conclusions, and present initial work and speculation; they state that a lot of work remains before a completely fair comparison between ResearchCyc and the ATP systems can be made, and that experiments on the entire FOLified KB would allow hundreds of queries to be run.
quotes: At the time of publication, we were unable to obtain the kind of extensive results that would enable us to draw conﬁdent conclusions.
a lot of work remains to be done before a completely fair comparison can be made between ResearchCyc and the ATP systems
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the limit of their results in Sections 5 and 6.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that the types of problems Cyc is designed to handle differ substantially from the types of problems the ATP systems are designed to handle, and state that state-of-the-art provers are optimized for mathematical problems requiring deep inference such as those in TPTP, on which Cyc would almost certainly perform very poorly. This second statement is not tested in the paper.
assertions.anchor: Section 1, p.2; Section 5.1, p.7; Section 6, p.8
quotes: we conclude that the types of problems Cyc is designed to handle differ substantially from the types of problems that the ATP systems are designed to handle
Cyc would almost certainly perform very poorly on those problems
assertions.certainty_reason: An author conclusion; the Cyc-on-TPTP claim has no evidence in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that ResearchCyc is available under a restricted but free license to all research institutions and universities, that the complete Cyc KB is under a proprietary license, and that OpenCyc is the open-source version of a subset (mostly the upper ontology) distributed under the Creative Commons license.
quotes: ResearchCyc is available under a restricted but free license to all research institutions and universities.
The complete Cyc knowledge base is under a proprietary license
OpenCycTM(www.opencyc.org) is the open-source version of a subset of the Cyc KB (mostly the upper ontology) freely distributed under the Creative Commons license.
assertions.certainty_reason: Cycorp authors describe the licensing of their own product in 2005.
assertions.reader_inference: A 2005 licensing statement; current terms may differ.

assertions.value: The authors state future work: set up experiments with a large corpus of ResearchCyc test-suite queries, explore incorporating theorem-proving strategies that beat Cyc on some query classes into ResearchCyc as HL modules, and generate a suite of common-sense benchmark problems from the ResearchCyc KB, which they have discussed with the maintainers of the TPTP library. They pose as open questions whether a first-order prover can efficiently answer realistic common-sense queries over a large KB.
quotes: we would like to explore the possibility of incorporating these methods into ResearchCyc, perhaps as HL modules
We have discussed with the maintainers of the TPTP problem library the possibility of generating a suite of common-sense benchmark problems from the ResearchCyc KB.
Is it possible to design a ﬁrstorder theorem prover that can efﬁciently answer realistic common-sense queries over a large KB?
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state open problems and planned work in Section 6.

assertions.value: The authors cite Reif and Schellhorn (1997) for the observation that goal-directed strategies are the only practical methods when the number of axioms is more than a few hundred, and describe common-sense queries as typically needing shallow inferences that use a very small percentage of the KB.
quotes: It has been observed (Reif & Schellhorn 1997) that goal-directed strategies are the only practical methods to use when the numbers of axioms are more than a few hundred.
proofs that use a very small percentage of the entire KB and do not have many steps
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work.
